question: to the Commission Nikolas Farantouris (S&D), Yannis Maniatis (S&D), Nikos Papandreou (S&D), Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

On 26 February 2026, the Single-Member Misdemeanour Court of Athens issued a landmark decision on the wiretapping scandal, finding the defendants guilty and imposing a total prison sentence of 126 years and 8 months1. At the same time, the case file was forwarded again to the prosecutorial authorities due to sufficient evidence of serious criminal acts despite the previous archiving of the case, given the volume of new evidence that emerged. However, on 27 April 2026, the Prosecutor of the Supreme Court (who, as supervising prosecutor of Greece’s national intelligence agency, had signed off the surveillance of eleven individuals who were also targets of Predator2) decided not to retrieve the case from the archive and, therefore, not to order any further investigation3. This decision has provoked strong reactions from society, the political world and the Bar Associations4. Given that, on the basis of the Commission's annual reports on the rule of law, the perceived independence of the judiciary in Greece has been continuously declining in recent years5: 1.
Does the Commission consider that the practices complained of and the absence of a substantive judicial investigation are in line with Greece's obligations under EU law6?

Does the Commission intend to include, in its forthcoming report on the rule of law in Greece, specific findings and recommendations to ensure the independence and impartiality of the prosecution, the effective investigation of the wiretapping scandal and Greece’s full compliance with EU law?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Commission does not comment on investigations and proceedings before national courts in individual cases. In general, as the Commission has stated on numerous occasions, it strongly condemns any illegal access to interpersonal communications. The EU has a strong legal framework for data protection and privacy when the use of spyware falls with the scope of EU law. The Commission’s annual Rule of Law Report monitors and reports on developments, with allegations of illegal use of spyware taken into consideration when relevant under the framework of national checks and balances, the protection of journalists and the safeguarding of media freedom. The Commission continues monitoring the situation of the rule of law in all Member States including Greece in the context of the 2026 Rule of Law Report, which is set for publication in July 2026.
